content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to use a skill graph to rapidly obtain policies in new environments. It is demonstrated in quadrupedal locomotion tasks, ranging from different speeds to different terrains.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pro:

1. Use of a skill graph for rapid adaptation of quadrupedal locomotion is new and interesting.

Con:

1. "We also do not need the simulation, thus bypassing the notorious reality gap problem (Koos et al., 2010)." A lot of sim-to-real research has happened in the past few years, especially for quadrupedal locomotion. Sim-to-real can now tackle much more challenging scenarios demonstrated in this paper.

2. It seems inefficient to store and search for all the skills. Since the robot/task/environment parameters are continuous, why not just fit a neural network so one policy can handle them all?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Few details are given about how the skill graph is initially constructed. Otherwise, the proposed method makes sense and seems straightforward to implement.
content.summary_of_the_review:
While this paper presents a new method to rapidly train policies for quadruped to adapt to new environments. The considered scenario is pretty simple compared to what is demonstrated in recent work. It is also unclear to me the scalability and efficiency of the proposed method when facing more challenging scenarios.

Here are more questions to be addressed during the rebuttal:

1. Please provide more details on how the skill graph is initially constructed. For example, how many samples are collected? How are they collected? 

2. I am confused about the comparison in Table 2. Does the proposed method learn 844 skills from scratch using only 10 minutes of real robot samples? If so, it is amazing but it sounds unlikely (but if it is I apologize). Otherwise, I am not sure why it is a fair comparison with other methods when most of them are learning from scratch.

3. Another interpretation of Table 2 is that the proposed method can learn 844 new skills based on some initial skill graphs. But it seems easy for other papers to start from some initial policy and fine-tune as well. A more interesting and insightful comparison will be comparing with other fintuning mechanisms, e.g., distilling all the policies in the skill graph into one single policy and fine-tune that policy in new environments.

4.   Figure 4 results seem obvious, a policy learned from scratch from SAC will clearly not perform better with finetuning a policy that is already capable of some similar tasks. Am I missing something here?

5. The text in Figure 2 is too small.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposed a method for training quadruped locomotion controllers. The core idea is to build a skill graph where each node in the graph represents a task, a robot, and an environment. During deployment, a skill that is closest to the deployment situation is selected and deployed. The collected data is then used in an off-line RL training to improve the policy performance. The method is applied to train a quadruped robot to walk in different directions and velocities on a few different terrains.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
strengths:
1. Using a graph to represent multiple skills for a robot is an interesting idea
2. Have some real-world results

weakensses
1. The paper is not very easy to read and various details are missing or hard to find. More details provided in the next question.
2. Retrieving a skill from the SG seems to require full knowledge of the testing setup, e.g. environment parameters, which is not usually available.
3. The presented controller (in my understanding) is a joystick controller that can be trained fairly easily with existing methods (e.g. rapid motor adaptation (RMA) has demonstrated a much wider set of skills). In addition the motion shown in the video doesn't seem to have very high quality: in the text the commanded velocity can be >1m/s but the video appears to be ~0.5m/s.
4. The presented environments seems to be mostly flat in general. It's not sure how well the method would work if a more unstructured outdoor environment is presented as it will deviate significantly from the existing skills.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I have a few clarification questions for the paper:
1) How is the first set of skills acquired? Is it starting from 5-10 minutes of random movement, or the initial dataset is collected using some pre-trained policies?
2) For collecting 5-10 minutes of data, is it done for each new skill, i.e. to learn 100 skills it takes 500-1000 minutes of data? Or the authors were able to train all 844 skills with 5-10 minutes in total? If not, what's the total robot time needed to obtain the given SG?
3) For the graphs of the two quadruped robots, do they share nodes somehow? Or they are completely isolated (i.e. it's equivalent to build two separate SGs for two robots)?
content.summary_of_the_review: My main concerns for the paper are that 1) many important details are not very clear from the text, which makes it hard to judge the quality and result of the work, 2) the presented locomotion results do not seem agile and are limited to relatively flat environments, especially when compared to state-of-the-art simulation-based methods. Thus I'm leaning towards rejection at the current stage.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The idea of a Skill Graph (SG) is proposed for fast quadruped adaptation of a skill, s, for a quadruped agent, A, 
to new environments, E. Instead of learning policies, the idea is to select from existing learned policies.
More formally, the skill graph stores (A,E,s) tuples, which represent policies that are originally trained via SAC.
As per Algorith 1, existing skills are retrieved by searching for matches for the desired agent, A, and 
environment, E, and returning the most similar skill.  If E itself is new, the most similar skill of the 
most similar environment is returned.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- transfer learning, sim-to-real, and generalization across skills (tasks) are important important problems
  in RL in general, and quadruped control provides a practical and challenging domain for testing ideas
  related to these problems.

Weaknesses:
- the writing leaves me highly uncertain about the actual method
- the method appears to be a form of table-lookup of precomputed policies;
  this is possibly a very practical approach, but has limited novelty and is a very constrained form of generalization
- some of the baseline comparisons are not meaningful, as they are design to learn from scratch,
  whereas the current method draws on a family of pretrained controllers
- the paper makes very large claims that are not supported, or that are supported via misleading comparisons.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The work could not be reproduced. Many details are missing, including how environments are categorized, how similarity is computed, what the perceptual capabilities of the quadrupeds are, and more.

The paper makes large claims about sim-to-real and learning from very few samples. These are either not supported, or are misleading in practice, i.e., the method appears to rely on a large library of precomputed policies.

I found the paper to be confusing with respect to the methodology and evaluations. It is unclear what conclusions the reader should draw from the various skill-graph visualizations.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper is unfortunately not ready for publication.  It is confusing and vague with respect to the vocabulary used, e.g., skills, environments.  There is likely more going on, but the method appears to be a form of table lookup of existing policies. The definitions of similarity between skills and between environments are given only in vague terms.  It was unclear to this reader what the 844 defined discrete skills were, on which the policy builds, and why discrete skills are needed when a more common solution is to develop policies that are conditioned on the appropriate task and environmental variables.

Hopefully these comments will be of help in improving future versions of this work.
------------------------------

It is unclear how the layout of the visualized skill graphs are determined, or why these skill graph 
illustrations would be an improvement over a table.

Terms such as "skills" and "environments" are not precisely defined, which makes it difficult to 
understand the exact scope of the problem being solved. 
The definition of "similarity" is also left undefined. 

The paper gives results for locomotion tasks, parameterized according to walking speed
and turning rate. This is a much narrower range of skills than might be expected with the rather large
claims being made in the abstract and introduction.

Much work on quadruped control learns a locomotion policy that can adapt to many environments by 
conditioning on the observation history, usually some combination of proprioception and other sensing
modalities.  Thus the environment is implicit in this observed history.  With this in mind, it is
not clear why representing environments as discrete entities would be a good idea. 
Relatedly, why should locomotion at different speeds be represented as discrete skill entities, when
a learned policy can simply condition on the desired target velocity?

L124: "Unlike these works, the SG we build will help agents quickly adapt to new and more difficult
real-world tasks."  I don't currently see the evidence for this.  The retrieval method that is being
proposed is not solving the same problem as the proposed baseline methods.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose a skill graph for fast quadruped locomotion skill learning and adaptation. Each element of the skill graph consists of the tri-elements: the robot type, the environment, and the skill (which is represented by the base motion tracking target). The skill graph can help accelerate real world locomotion skill learning in the following way: if the environment, robot, and locomotion tracking targets combination is found within the skill graph, the same policy/agent will be retrieved and re-used. If not, a closest policy will be used to fine tune in the new environment, and the fine tuned policy will be stored back to the skill graph. The authors show that their skill graph is more sample efficient than many baselines based on reported numbers.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The strengths of the paper:
1) The idea of using a skill graph to store locomotion policies is novel and can be potentially useful for many downstream tasks (more than just locomotion).  
2) Using real world collected offline data and also deployed back to the real world. 
3) Fast fine tuning of policies with limited samples in the real world. 

The weaknesses of the paper:
1) It is quite an exaggeration to claim “844” skills, since the difference between many skills are trivial (i.e. slightly different walking speed/angular velocities on mostly flat, hard grounds). Nowadays it is easy to train a single policy that can continuously track different base velocities and angular velocities on all these terrains without such a complex approach. 
2) Not clearly written and the reader has to guess many details. For example, by inferring from the whole paper I assume that the authors have to train a separate policy for each node in the graph, but is it the case? Also, what are the expert policies being used here? 
3) Comparison with baselines are done through reported numbers but not real experiments. I don’t think that is the right way to compare with these baselines because the experiment setups can be completely different and the definition of skills are also dramatically different.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is not quite clearly written with many missing details. The quality of the paper is questionable since the comparison with the baselines are done incorrectly. The paper does have some original ideas (i.e. use skill graph to store locomotion policies).
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper needs re-writing and the reported methods should be properly compared with baselines.
